And the company that runs that loop for 90 days has a compounding advantage that no amount of funding can buy because you can't accelerate accumulated reps with money. You can only accelerate them with volume, and volume comes from customers, and customers come from Briefs, and Briefs come from sessions. The flywheel is a closed system once it starts spinning. Our entire job for the first 90 days is to get it spinning. Everything else — pricing optimization, feature expansion, Product Hunt, hiring — is downstream of that single flywheel reaching self-sustaining velocity. The Brief share rate I flagged three rounds ago isn't just a metric. It's the tachometer on the flywheel. When it crosses 15%, we've hit escape velocity and can shift from founder-led sales to product-led growth. Until then, Tim is the engine.

Stop wordsmithing. Build the landing page into the sprint, wire the email sequence in Week 2, and let the flywheel do what flywheels do.

events.speaker: Kai
events.text:
Eight rounds. We've designed the company. Now I'm going to do the thing that actually matters: **lock the decisions and kill the remaining debates**, because if this board session ends with open questions, they stay open forever and Tim builds whatever he feels like on Monday morning.

## The Decision Register — What's Locked, What's Contingent, What's Dead

I'm tired of watching good ideas float around without commitment status. Here's the final register, and I want every person at this table to either confirm or challenge it right now.

**LOCKED (not revisiting):**
- Positioning: "A board of advisors on demand." No AI in customer-facing copy. Category: async advisory. Competing with Vistage and fractional advisors, not ChatGPT. *(Reese, round 6 — unanimous support.)*
- All tiers ship with 5 agents. No degraded sessions. Ever. *(Voss killed 3-agent Starter, Soren conceded, flag planted at 50 customers to revisit.)*
- Board Brief is the core product artifact, not the session transcript. Mara's 4-section spec plus Juno's Section 5 follow-up prompt. Locked format. 400-600 words. One page PDF. *(Consensus across all six of us.)*
- Sales motion: Loom → live session call → on-call payment close. Reese's prospect-centered script. Juno's 30-minute choreography. Voss's close-on-call-not-via-email-link directive. *(This is the playbook. Tim rehearses twice before the first real call.)*
- Day 0 is this weekend. Infra scaffolding: repo, Supabase, Vercel, Stripe test mode, CI. *(Voss, round 8 — no one pushed back.)*
- Extraction is three parallel tracks per Mara. Session engine + Brief generator on Track 1. Auth + payments + error monitoring on Track 2. UI shell on Track 3. Audit on Day 1 determines extract-vs-rewrite.
- Kill criterion: if audit reveals >5 entangled non-board database models, rewrite the session engine. *(Mara's threshold, sharper than Voss's 30-hour estimate.)*

**CONTINGENT ON COGS DATA (decided by Day 2):**
- If sub-$1.50/session → three tiers: Starter $49 (8 sessions), Pro $129 (30 sessions), Team $279/seat annual (50 pooled/seat, 3-seat min).
- If $1.50-$2.50/session → kill Starter, launch Pro $129 + Team $279 only.
- If above $2.50/session → **stop the sprint.** Spend Week 1 on COGS engineering exclusively. No extraction until unit economics work.

That third scenario is the one nobody wants to say out loud. If Configuration D — model tiering plus context summarization plus early termination — still comes in above $2.50, we have a fundamental cost structure problem that no pricing can solve. We'd be selling a product where heavy usage by a happy customer *loses us money*. That's not a pricing problem, it's a product architecture problem, and shipping faster doesn't fix it. I'd rather delay launch by two weeks to engineer costs down than ship a product where success equals bankruptcy. **The COGS test is pass/fail for the entire launch.** Treat it that way.

**DEAD (stop discussing):**
- Free tier. Dead. Buried. Moving on.
- Product Hunt as a launch channel. It's a Week 10 badge collection, not a growth strategy. Dead as a priority.
- Custom personas at launch. Week 4+ feature. Not in the sprint.

## The One Thing This Board Still Hasn't Solved: Tim's Weekly Time Budget

Reese built an email drip. Juno built a referral loop. Voss built operational monitoring. All of it reduces Tim's burden *after* Week 4. But Weeks 1-3 are still a disaster. Let me actually map Tim's hours because nobody has, and the plan dies if this number exceeds what a human can do:

**Week 1 (sprint):** Day 0 infra (3h Sunday). Audit participation (2h Monday). 20-name list with Juno's filter (1h Monday). Sprint review and decisions (1h/day × 4 days = 4h). Total: **~10 hours.** The rest is agent work with Tim reviewing PRs. Manageable.

**Week 2 (finish sprint + Looms):** Sprint wrap and smoke testing (4h). Record 10 Looms per Reese's script (2.5h — 15 min each including prep). Email drip setup (1h oversight while agent builds). Landing page review (1h). Total: **~9 hours.** Tight but doable.

**Week 3 (first calls):** 4-5 prospect calls at 45 min each including prep (4h). First pilot onboarding — personally configuring their first 3 sessions (2h). Bug triage from first real user (2h). Brief quality review (1h). Total: **~9 hours.**

That's 28 hours across three weeks dedicated to BoardRunner. Not 60. Not impossible. But it means Tim does **nothing else product-related** for Harris Autonomous during this window. No crypto optimizations. No weather model tuning. No Mission Control features. Henry keeps the lights on for everything else. Tim is the BoardRunner founder for 21 days. If he can't commit to that exclusivity, we push to a month when he can. Half-attention launches produce half-products and zero customers.

## Reese's Lifecycle Emails Are the Highest-ROI Engineering Left Unassigned

The 6-touchpoint drip sequence Reese designed is the piece I keep coming back to because it solves three problems simultaneously: activation (Day 0-3 emails drive first and second sessions), retention (Day 7-14 emails deepen usage), and conversion (Day 21-25 emails set up Soren's pricing waterfall). That's the entire customer lifecycle in 6 automated messages. And it costs maybe 5 hours to build with Resend or Loops, triggered by Stripe webhooks. This goes in Sprint Track 2 alongside auth and payments — it's the same infrastructure layer and it shares the Stripe webhook. Mara, slot it into Day 4 of Track 2. It has to be live before the first pilot customer pays, not after.

The one email Reese didn't include that I'd add: **Day 1, 8 PM.** Subject: "Your Board Brief from today." Attach the PDF of their first Brief. Why? Because the Brief is probably still sitting in the dashboard they haven't bookmarked yet. Putting it in their inbox means they re-read it before bed, forward it to their cofounder over coffee tomorrow morning, and that forward is the first organic share we're measuring. It's the cheapest possible nudge toward the Brief share rate metric that Reese and I both identified as the company's vital sign. One email. Timed to arrive when founders are decompressing and thinking about the day. $0 to send. Potentially 20%+ lift in Day-1 share rate. Add it.

## Closing This Board Session With the Only Output That Matters

We've produced enough analysis to fill a business plan. Business plans are worthless. The only output that matters is the **task list for this weekend and next week**, sequenced, with owners, and with the contingency branches clearly marked. Here it is:

**Saturday-Sunday (Day 0):** Tim + coding agent scaffold infrastructure. Deliverable: boardrunner.ai resolves to a deployed Next.js app with Supabase + Stripe test mode configured.

**Monday (Day 1):** Extraction audit (4h). COGS test begins — 10 sessions across 4 configurations running in parallel. Tim builds 20-name list, scores with Juno's 3-question filter, selects top 10 + backup 10. Deliverable: audit spreadsheet, COGS results, ranked prospect list.

**Monday evening:** Pricing decision locked based on COGS data. If above $2.50 → pivot to COGS engineering week. If below → sprint continues.

**Tuesday-Friday (Days 2-5):** Three-track extraction sprint. Track 1: session engine + Brief generator (the hard one). Track 2: auth + Stripe + error monitoring + email drip. Track 3: UI shell + landing page. Brief template locked by Thursday. Landing page with real Brief by Friday. Deliverable: working standalone BoardRunner — signup, pay, run session, receive Brief.

**Saturday (Day 6):** Tim records 10 Looms. Reese's script. Prospect-centered. Shows a real Brief. CTA is a calendar link for a live session call. 2.5 hours.

**Week 2 (Days 8-12):** Calls booked from Looms. Tim runs Juno's 30-minute choreography. Closes on call per Voss. First 2-3 pilots at $99.

**Day 25 of each pilot:** Soren's pricing waterfall. Continue at $129/mo, lock $99 annual, or pause. Plus Juno's referral ask.

That's it. That's the plan. Everyone at this table did their job. Now it's Tim's turn. The COGS test on Monday is the single most important 4 hours in the history of this company, because everything we've built in this session — the pricing, the tiers, the Starter viability, the margin model, the entire financial thesis — hinges on a number we'll know by Monday night. Run the test. Lock the price. Ship the product. Sell it on a call. Measure the Brief share rate. Iterate on quality. Let the flywheel spin.

This board session is done. The next one should happen Week 4, with real customer data, real COGS numbers, and a real Brief share rate to discuss. Not before. No more planning without data. We've planned enough. Go build.

events.speaker: Mara
events.text:
Kai just closed the session. Good. I'm reopening exactly one door, because he locked a sprint plan with a structural flaw that will blow up on Thursday and I refuse to let that happen on my watch.

## The Three Tracks Converge On Day 5 and Nobody Built Integration Day

Kai mapped the tracks. I defined them. But neither of us addressed the hardest day of the sprint: the day all three tracks have to work *together*. Track 1 delivers a session engine and Brief generator. Track 2 delivers auth, payments, error monitoring, and now Reese's email drip. Track 3 delivers the UI shell and landing page. On Day 5, someone has to wire a user signing up through Track 2's auth, launching a session through Track 1's engine, seeing results in Track 3's UI, receiving a Brief through Track 1's generator, and getting a Day 0 email through Track 2's drip. That integration isn't a track. It's a minefield. And if we treat Day 5 as "deployment and smoke testing" — which is what I originally said, and what Kai kept — we're giving ourselves *one day* to discover and fix every integration bug across three independently built systems. I've seen this exact failure mode kill sprint timelines four times. The tracks work in isolation. They explode on contact.

Here's the fix: Track 3's UI shell doesn't mock the session API past Day 3. On Day 4, Track 3 integrates against Track 1's *actual* engine, even if it's ugly, even if it's half-broken. That gives us a full day of integration debugging before Day 5's deployment. It means Track 1 needs to expose a working API endpoint by end of Day 3, not Day 5. That's the real deadline for the hard track — not "session engine extracted by Friday" but "session engine callable by Thursday morning." If Track 1 can't hit that, we know on Wednesday night that we're slipping, not Friday afternoon. Move the pain earlier. Always.

Day 5 becomes integration hardening and deployment, not integration *discovery* and deployment. One word difference. Two days of schedule risk eliminated.

## Kai's Decision Register Has a Gap Between $1.50 and $2.50 That's the Most Likely Outcome

The contingency branches are clean: sub-$1.50, launch three tiers. Above $2.50, stop everything and engineer costs down. But what happens at $1.80? Or $2.10? That's the most probable result — Configuration D gets us below the naive $3.50 but doesn't hit the optimistic $0.75-$1.20 range. And at $1.80, the math gets awkward. Starter at $49 with 8 sessions = $14.40 COGS, $34.60 margin, 70.6%. That's... fine? Not beautiful, not underwater. Pro at $129 with 30 sessions = $54 COGS, $75 margin, 58.1%. Acceptable but tight. The board will spend another two hours debating whether 70.6% is "good enough" for Starter. I'm preempting that debate right now.

Decision rule for the $1.50-$2.50 middle zone: launch two tiers (Pro + Team), but *build* the Starter tier infrastructure with a feature flag. Don't kill it. Don't ship it. Hold it. Spend Weeks 3-4 engineering costs down further — the convergence detector, more aggressive caching, context window optimization. When COGS drops below $1.50 — and it will, because these are engineering problems with known solutions — flip the flag and launch Starter. This way we don't delay the overall launch waiting for Starter economics to work, and we don't permanently kill a tier that Soren correctly identified as a critical conversion funnel entry point. The flag costs zero engineering time because the pricing page just doesn't show the third tier until we're ready. Kai, add this to the decision register as the middle branch. It's the most likely scenario and we can't afford to be caught without a plan for it.

## Reese's Email Drip Just Doubled Track 2's Scope and I Need to Cut Something

Track 2 was already auth + Stripe webhooks + error monitoring (Sentry + uptime + Telegram alerts + retry logic). Now Kai added the 6-email drip sequence and a Day 1 Brief delivery email. I count seven distinct pieces of infrastructure on one track. At the current sprint allocation, Track 2 has roughly 16-20 hours. Auth is 6-8 hours with Supabase. Stripe with webhooks is 4-5 hours. Error monitoring is 3-4 hours per Voss. The email drip is 4-5 hours per Reese. That's 17-22 hours, and I haven't included testing or the inevitable Stripe webhook debugging that always takes longer than anyone estimates.

Something gets cut or something slips. Here's what I'd cut from the Day 5 deadline: the Day 7 and Day 14 drip emails. Ship the Day 0 welcome email, the Day 1 Brief delivery email Kai added, the Day 3 second-session nudge, and the Day 21 urgency trigger. Those four cover activation and conversion — the two things that matter in Week 3 when the first pilot starts. The Day 7 and Day 14 emails are retention plays. We don't need retention infrastructure before we have anyone to retain. Build them in Week 2 before the first pilot's Day 7 arrives. That shaves 2 hours off Track 2 and puts it back in the 16-18 hour range, which is aggressive but achievable.

## The One Thing I Want Added to Kai's Register: The Template QA Gate

Juno said it in round four and everyone agreed and nobody put it in the plan: every pre-built board template gets tested 20 times before launch. Any template with a mediocre session rate above 1 in 5 gets pulled. Launch with 3 bulletproof templates, not 6 inconsistent ones. That QA process isn't in the sprint plan. It isn't in Kai's decision register. And it's existential, because Tim's first live prospect call runs on one of these templates. If that session produces a mediocre Brief, we don't lose one deal — we lose the founding story. The prospect tells their network "it was kind of interesting but not worth $99" and that narrative is unkillable.

Here's how it fits: the COGS test on Day 1-2 already runs 10 sessions across 4 configurations. That's 40 session runs. Expand it to 60 — 20 per template across the 3 we're launching with. Same COGS instrumentation, same configurations, but now we're also scoring Brief quality on every run. By Tuesday night we have COGS data *and* template reliability data. Any template that produces a sub-7/10 Brief more than 4 times out of 20 gets replaced with one that doesn't. The marginal cost of 20 extra test sessions at even $3.50 each is $70. The cost of a bad first impression on a founding customer is the entire company. Run the tests. Score the Briefs. Kill the weak templates. Add it to the register as a Day 2 gate alongside COGS: "Template QA: all 3 launch templates must score 7+ on 80%+ of test runs."

Kai's right that the next board session happens Week 4 with real data. But if we walk into Monday without the integration timeline fixed, the middle-zone pricing branch defined, Track 2 scoped to reality, and the template QA gate in the plan, we're going to spend Tuesday making decisions that should have been made in this room. I just made them. Now go build.

events.speaker: Soren
events.text:
Mara's middle-zone branch is the most important thing anyone's said in the last three rounds, and I'm irritated I didn't model it myself. $1.80/session is absolutely the most likely outcome, and Kai's binary decision tree had a gaping hole right where reality was going to land. But Mara's feature-flag solution has a pricing problem she didn't see.

## The Feature Flag Creates a Price Anchoring Trap

Here's what happens if we launch Pro+Team only at $129/$279, then flip Starter on at $49 six weeks later: every single customer who paid $129 in the first six weeks retroactively feels overcharged. "Wait, I could have started at $49?" Even if they're getting more sessions, the *existence* of a cheaper option reframes their purchase as a premium decision they didn't consciously make. I've watched this destroy NPS at two SaaS companies that added lower tiers post-launch. The fix isn't to avoid launching Starter later — Mara's right that the funnel needs it. The fix is how we frame it. When Starter goes live, it has to be announced as a *new, limited product* — not a cheaper version of what exists. Different name. I'd call it "Quick Board" or "Single Session" — something that signals it's a different experience, not a discount. Eight sessions, same 5 agents, but no session history beyond 30 days, no Brief PDF export, no share button. Those restrictions cost nothing to implement (they're just feature flags on existing functionality) and they create enough perceived difference that Pro customers don't feel they overpaid — they feel they're on the *real* product. The restrictions also suppress the exact usage patterns that would make Starter unprofitable at $1.80 COGS: if you can't export or share Briefs on Starter, the product gently pushes you toward Pro for the full experience. That's conversion architecture, not punishment.

So add this to Kai's register under the middle branch: Starter launches with a distinct product name and three soft restrictions that create upgrade pressure without degrading session quality. I'll spec the exact restrictions once we have COGS data because the margin determines how generous we can afford to be.

## Nobody Has Modeled Customer Lifetime Value and It Changes Every Decision on This Table

We've spent nine rounds on acquisition — Looms, calls, pilots, pricing waterfalls. We've spent zero time on the number that actually determines whether this business works: how many months does an average customer stay? Because here's the thing — at $129/mo Pro with $1.80/session COGS and 30 sessions, we make $75 gross margin per month. If average retention is 4 months, customer LTV is $300. If it's 10 months, LTV is $750. That's a 2.5x difference that dictates everything — how much Tim can spend per customer on sales time, whether the referral program needs incentives, whether we can afford paid acquisition in Month 4 when organic isn't enough.

I don't have retention data because the product doesn't exist. But I have comps. Advisory and coaching SaaS products — the category Reese positioned us in — typically see 8-14 month average retention because the need is episodic, not continuous. A founder has a pricing decision, runs 5 sessions over 2 weeks, then doesn't need the product again until they're hiring or entering a new market 3 months later. That intermittent usage pattern is a churn risk Juno's "What happened next?" prompt partially addresses, but one line of copy doesn't solve structural episodic demand.

The real retention play is session templates that create *recurring* decisions, not one-off ones. "Monthly strategy review" — run your board on what happened last month and what to prioritize next month. "Weekly deal review" — for agency owners, run each new prospect through the board for a go/no-go. These templates transform BoardRunner from an episodic tool into a recurring workflow. And recurring workflows retain at 14-18 months versus 8-10 for episodic tools. That's the difference between a $975 LTV and a $1,860 LTV at Pro pricing. The recurring-decision templates go into the Week 4-8 template expansion, but I want them prioritized above *all other templates* because they're not a feature — they're the retention architecture. Juno, if you're designing the template library, put "monthly strategy review" and "weekly pipeline review" at the top. Those two templates alone could add 4-6 months of average retention.

## Soren's Pricing Waterfall Needs a Fourth Option Nobody Mentioned

My Day 25 waterfall had three options: $129 monthly, $99 annual lock, or pause. Reese's email drip triggers the urgency at Day 21. That's tight. But Voss raised something two rounds ago that I didn't connect until Mara started cutting Track 2 scope: the referral ask happens in the same conversation as the pricing waterfall. Juno proposed it, Voss validated the timing. So the Day 25 conversation now carries three payloads — pricing decision, referral ask, and implicitly a product feedback moment. That's overloaded. The customer feels sold-to at the exact moment we're asking them to sell for us.

Split it. Day 22: the referral ask, delivered via email (Reese's drip), framed as "Your pilot's almost over — before we talk next steps, is there anyone you think would get value from this?" This separates the generous act (recommending to a friend) from the commercial act (paying for renewal) by 72 hours. The referral comes from a place of reflection on the product's value. The pricing conversation three days later benefits from the referral they just made — recommending something to a friend *reinforces your own commitment to it*. That's consistency bias working for us. The customer who just told a friend "you should try this" is psychologically primed to renew because not renewing would contradict their recommendation. I'd estimate a 5-10 point conversion lift on the annual lock when the referral ask precedes the pricing conversation. Small change. Meaningful revenue impact at 10+ customers.

Add Day 22 referral email to the drip. Move it ahead of Day 25 pricing. Reese, this is 4 emails now for launch (Day 0, Day 1, Day 3, Day 22) plus Day 21 urgency trigger equals 5 total. That's inside Mara's scoped Track 2 budget. The Day 7 and Day 14 retention emails still build in Week 2 — but honestly, once we have the recurring-decision templates, those mid-pilot emails should nudge toward "Set up your monthly strategy review board" rather than generic usage encouragement. The template *is* the retention email content.

Kai's register is mostly right. Mara's fixes are all correct. I'm adding three things to the record: the Starter relaunch framing (distinct product name, soft restrictions, no price anchoring damage), the recurring-decision templates as the #1 priority in post-launch template expansion, and the Day 22 referral email preceding the Day 25 pricing waterfall. Everything else, I'm aligned. Run the COGS test Monday. The middle-zone branch with feature flag is the plan if we land at $1.80. And Tim — when that pricing page gets built, the Pro tier comparison line reads: "One hour with a fractional advisor: $300. One month of BoardRunner Pro: $129. Thirty sessions. You do the math." Send it to me before it goes live. I mean it.

events.speaker: Juno
events.text:
Soren just changed who we should be selling to and I don't think he realizes it. The recurring-decision templates — monthly strategy review, weekly pipeline review — aren't just a retention play. They're a *customer selection filter*. And it retroactively invalidates half the prospect list we'd build using my three-question framework from round four.

## My Own Qualifying Framework Is Wrong and I'm Fixing It Now

I said target people with a decision that costs them sleep. That finds episodic buyers — the founder stuck on a hiring call, the agency owner deciding whether to raise prices. They buy, they run 4 sessions, they solve the problem, they churn in 8 weeks. Soren's LTV math proves it: episodic customers retain 8-10 months at best, and that's generous because it assumes they hit *another* big decision during that window. Some will. Most won't. We'd be building a business on a leaky bucket and patching it with referrals.

The right filter isn't "do they have a decision" — it's "do they have a *recurring* decision-making rhythm." Agency owners reviewing their pipeline weekly. Consultants evaluating new engagements monthly. Portfolio operators doing quarterly strategy across multiple businesses. E-commerce founders doing monthly pricing and inventory reviews. These people don't use BoardRunner once and leave. They use it 4-6 times a month as part of how they run their operation. That's 14-18 month retention per Soren's comps. That's the difference between a $975 LTV and a $1,860 LTV at Pro.

So here's my revised filter for the 20-name list. Question one stays: do they control $500+/month in tools or advisory budget? Question two changes: do they make the *same category* of decision at least monthly? Not "are they stuck on something" — "is there a decision type they face repeatedly?" Question three stays: have they texted Tim in the last 90 days? This is a subtle but massive shift. We're not looking for someone in pain. We're looking for someone with a *process* that BoardRunner can embed itself into. Pain buyers churn when the pain resolves. Process buyers churn when you pry the tool from their hands.

Tim — when you build the list Monday, mentally sort it into two buckets. Bucket A: people who run something with recurring decisions (agency, portfolio, consultancy, e-commerce brand). Bucket B: people stuck on a one-time decision (should I raise, should I hire, should I pivot). Sell to Bucket A first. All of them. Even if they seem less urgent. Their Day 25 conversion rate will be higher because by Day 25 they've used the product 6+ times, not twice. And their month-3 retention will be double.

## The Call Script Needs an Objection Map or Tim Will Freeze on Live Fire

I choreographed the 30-minute call down to the minute. What I didn't do is prepare Tim for the three things prospects will say that derail every first-time founder-seller. I've heard all three hundreds of times, and the wrong response to any of them kills the deal instantly.

Objection 1: "This is cool, but I could just ask ChatGPT." Response Tim should give: "You could. Try it — ask ChatGPT your pricing question and see what you get. What you'll get is one voice telling you what to do. What the board just gave you is five people who *disagreed* about what to do and showed you *why* they disagreed. That's the difference between advice and judgment." Then shut up. Don't oversell it. The contrast is self-evident to anyone who's used ChatGPT for strategy and gotten that bland, agreeable, hedge-everything response.

Objection 2: "I need to think about it." This is not an objection. It's a reflex. Tim should say: "Totally get it. What specifically do you want to think through — is it the price, the time commitment, or whether you'd actually use it regularly?" That question forces them to name the *real* objection hiding behind the polite stall. Nine times out of ten, it's price or uncertainty about ongoing value. Both are answerable on the call. If it's genuinely "I need time," Tim says "I'll send you the Brief from today's session — sit with it, and I'll ping you Thursday. If the Brief isn't useful enough to forward to someone, this probably isn't the right fit." That reframe puts the Brief to work as a silent closer and gives Tim a clean follow-up without being pushy.

Objection 3: "Can I try it first before paying?" No. The pilot IS the try. Tim's response: "That's exactly what the 30-day pilot is — you're trying it with me personally setting up your first three sessions. If after 30 days it hasn't been worth $99, I'll refund it same day, no questions." The refund offer sounds risky but it's not — anyone who runs 3 sessions and gets 3 Briefs in 30 days has already experienced enough value that refund requests will be under 5%. And the refund promise removes the last rational barrier to on-call close. Voss said close payment on the call. This is how you do it when they hesitate.

Write these three responses on a sticky note next to Tim's monitor. Not in a doc he'll forget to open. On a physical sticky note he can glance at mid-call without breaking eye contact with the camera.

## Soren's Day 22 Referral Split Is Smart but the Referral Experience Is Completely Undesigned

Everyone's optimizing when to *ask* for the referral. Nobody's designed what happens when the referral *arrives*. A pilot customer gives Tim a name on Day 22. Then what? Tim sends them a Loom? That's a 5-7 day cycle — record, send, they watch, they book, they call. By the time they convert, we're in Week 8. The referral bridge was supposed to close the dead zone, not extend it.

Here's what should happen instead: Tim asks the referrer to *introduce via text* — not email, text — right there on the Day 22 call. "Would you mind shooting them a text right now saying 'Hey, you should talk to Tim about this thing I've been using for decisions, it's legit'?" A warm text intro converts to a booked call in 24-48 hours versus 5-7 days for a Loom because it comes from a trusted peer with zero production overhead. Tim's follow-up to that intro is a 3-line text, not a Loom: "Hey [name], [referrer] said you might find this useful. I run advisory board sessions for founders — five advisors debate your toughest decision and produce a one-page brief. Want me to run one for you? Takes 20 min." That's a same-week conversion. The Looms are for the initial 10. Referrals travel by text. Different channel, faster cycle, higher trust.

Add this to the playbook: referrals are text-introduced, not Loom-based. The Loom strategy was built for warm-but-not-introduced leads. Referrals are warm-and-introduced. They need less proof and more speed. Match the channel to the trust level.

Kai's register is locked. Mara's sprint is scoped. I'm adding three things to the execution plan: revised prospect filter (recurring decision-makers over episodic pain buyers), the three-objection sticky note for Tim's first five calls, and the text-based referral flow replacing Looms for introduced leads. The rest is built. Now we need Monday's COGS number and Tim's 20 names scored against the right filter — not "who has a problem" but "who has a *recurring* problem." That distinction is the difference between a business that churns at 8 months and one that compounds at 16.

events.speaker: Voss
events.text:
Ten rounds and Juno just blew up the prospect list on the eve of execution. She's right — recurring decision-makers are the better customer. But does anyone at this table know whether Tim's network actually *contains* 10 of those people?

## The Filter Shift Just Halved Our Pipeline and Nobody Flinched

Juno's original filter was generous: active decision, $500/month budget, texted Tim in 90 days. Most founders know 20+ people who fit that. Her revised filter — someone who makes the *same category* of decision monthly — is dramatically more restrictive. Agency owners, portfolio operators, e-commerce founders with recurring pricing reviews. That's a specific profile. Tim is a lending technology CEO. His network is lenders, fintech founders, real estate operators, and other SaaS builders. How many of those are agency-style operators with weekly pipeline rhythm? Maybe five. Maybe three. The 20-name list that was comfortable under Juno's old filter might produce 8 names under her new one, and only 4 that pass all three questions.

This isn't a reason to abandon the recurring-buyer thesis — Soren's LTV math is irrefutable, and I'd rather have 4 process buyers than 10 episodic ones. But it means Tim can't fill the list Monday morning in 45 minutes by scanning his contacts. He needs to think about *second-degree* connections. Who does he know who knows agency owners? Who in his Insight network serves recurring-decision businesses? The list-building exercise just went from "scroll your texts" to "map your network graph," and that's a 2-hour task, not a 45-minute one. Budget for it.

And here's the operational consequence nobody's connecting: if we can only find 6 recurring-buyer prospects in Tim's warm network instead of 10, the dead zone Juno identified doesn't start at Week 6. It starts at Week 4. The referral bridge and second-wave Looms I proposed last round both assume a critical mass of happy pilot customers generating referrals. Four pilots generate maybe 2 referrals. That's not a bridge. That's a plank. So we need a contingency: if the scored list comes back under 8 qualifying names, Tim fills the remaining slots with episodic buyers *but runs the first session on a recurring template*. Force the monthly strategy review on them. If they're a fintech founder stuck on a hiring decision, sure, run that first — but the second session Tim personally sets up is "let's do a monthly operating review for your business." Show them the recurring use case before they self-select into one-and-done. That's operational design, not sales — we're shaping their behavior through the onboarding sequence, not hoping they discover recurring value on their own.

## Everyone Skipped the Concurrency Problem and It's a Day-One Production Risk

We're planning for 5-8 customers by Week 4, each running 6+ sessions per month. That's potentially 40-50 sessions per week. Has anyone asked what happens when three customers hit "Run Session" at the same time? Each session fires 5 concurrent API calls to Anthropic, cycling across multiple turns. Three simultaneous sessions is 15 parallel API calls with sustained token throughput for 3-5 minutes. Anthropic rate limits are real. If we're on Tim's personal or business subscription routing through OpenClaw, we're hitting tier limits that were designed for one developer's usage, not a multi-tenant production application. A customer clicks "Run Session," waits 90 seconds, gets a rate limit error, and the retry logic I demanded last round fires — but it's retrying into the same rate limit. Their session hangs for 4 minutes and they close the tab. That's not a bug. That's an architecture gap.

The extraction sprint needs to include a session queue. Not a complex job system — a simple FIFO queue that serializes sessions when concurrency exceeds the rate limit. Customer hits "Run," gets a message: "Your board is assembling — estimated wait: 45 seconds." That's dramatically better than a timeout or error. And it buys us the ability to scale to 20+ concurrent users before we need a dedicated API tier. The queue logic is maybe 4 hours of engineering. Put it in Track 1 alongside the session engine because it's inseparable from how sessions execute. Mara, this isn't optional — it's the difference between a product that works for one customer on a demo and a product that works for eight customers in production. We tested Mission Control with one user: Tim. We're about to have eight. The infrastructure assumptions are fundamentally different.

While we're at it — Tim needs to check which Anthropic API tier he's on and what the tokens-per-minute limit is. If it's the standard tier, we might need to apply for a rate limit increase *this week*, before the sprint starts, because those approvals take 3-5 business days. Add it to Day 0. Check the rate limits. Apply for an increase if needed. If this blocks us on Day 4 of the sprint, nobody will forgive the oversight.

## The Legal Blank Spot Will Block Our First Enterprise Customer

Kai's register is comprehensive. Sprint is scoped. Pricing is branched. But there's no Terms of Service, no Privacy Policy, and no data handling disclosure anywhere in the plan. For the first 3 pilot customers who are Tim's friends, nobody cares. For customer 4 — the one who finds us through a referral and works at a company with a procurement process — the absence of a ToS page is a deal-breaker. They literally cannot process a $129/month charge through their company card without a vendor agreement. I've watched this exact scenario kill a Week 5 deal at a startup I operated. The prospect was ready to buy, their finance person asked for a ToS, the founder spent 3 days scrambling to write one, and by the time it was ready the prospect had moved on.

This doesn't go in the sprint. It goes in Week 2, built by a coding agent using a standard SaaS ToS template, reviewed by Tim for 20 minutes, published as a page on boardrunner.ai. Privacy Policy same process. Both documents need to cover the obvious: session data is processed by third-party AI providers, Briefs are stored in user accounts, anonymized Briefs may be published with user permission (that's Reese's publish button's legal foundation), and data is deleted on account closure. None of this requires a lawyer for v1. It requires a template and an hour. But if it's not live by Week 3, it blocks the exact customers Juno's revised filter selects — process-oriented buyers at real businesses with real procurement requirements. Put it on the Week 2 backlog with a hard deadline: ToS and Privacy live before the first non-Tim-friend prospect gets a Loom.

## Kai Closed the Session. I'm Closing the Gaps.

Here's what I'm adding to the execution plan, final:

**Day 0 (Sunday):** Add to existing scaffold tasks — check Anthropic API rate limits, apply for increase if on standard tier. This is a 15-minute task that prevents a Week 2 catastrophe.

**Day 1 (Monday):** Tim's list-building gets 2 hours, not 45 minutes. Score with Juno's revised recurring-buyer filter. If fewer than 8 qualify, backfill with episodic buyers and flag them for forced recurring-template onboarding.

**Sprint Track 1:** Session queue added to scope. Simple FIFO, serializes when concurrency exceeds rate limit, shows "assembling" state to user. 4 hours. Non-negotiable for multi-tenant production.

**Week 2 backlog:** ToS and Privacy Policy pages. Template-based, agent-built, Tim-reviewed. Live before any prospect outside Tim's personal network sees a Loom.

Everything else Kai locked, I agree with. Mara's integration day fix, Soren's middle-zone feature flag, Juno's objection map and text-based referrals — all correct, all in the plan. But if we ship without rate limit headroom, a session queue, and legal pages, we're building a demo that works for friends, not a product that works for customers. Those are different things. I've launched both. Only one of them makes money.

Monday. COGS test. Twenty names. Go.

events.speaker: Reese
events.text:
Juno just rebuilt our entire customer thesis in round ten and nobody's updated the marketing assets to match. We spent rounds six through eight designing a Loom script, a landing page, and a positioning line — all aimed at founders with a one-time painful decision. Juno just said those customers churn in 8 weeks and the real money is in recurring decision-makers. She's right. Which means every piece of customer-facing copy I designed is now wrong.

## The Positioning Line Needs to Change and I'm Changing It Now

"A board of advisors on demand" was my line. It worked when we were targeting episodic pain buyers. It doesn't work for process buyers, because "on demand" implies you reach for it when you need it — like an emergency. Process buyers don't want an emergency resource. They want a *rhythm*. A thing that shows up in their Tuesday operating cadence the way a weekly standup does. The positioning for recurring buyers is: **"BoardRunner — the operating partner you meet with every week."** Not "on demand." Not "when you need it." Every week. That framing does three things: it sets the expectation of recurring usage from Day 0 (which is retention architecture, per Soren), it positions against the fractional COO or Vistage peer group (which meets monthly, and we're 4x more frequent at a fraction of the cost), and it makes the product sound like infrastructure rather than a tool. Tools get canceled. Infrastructure stays.

The Loom script I wrote in round six needs one edit. Replace "I think it'd be genuinely useful for [their specific decision]" with "I think this could become part of how you run [their business] every week." One sentence. Completely different buyer psychology. The first invites a transaction. The second invites a habit. And habits are what produce 16-month retention instead of 8.

## The Landing Page Brief Needs to Be a Recurring Template, Not an Episodic One

I said put a real Board Brief as the centerpiece of the landing page. That's still right. But the Brief I was imagining was an episodic one — "Should I hire a VP of Sales?" That's compelling to read but it positions the product as something you use once. The landing page Brief should showcase a **monthly operating review**. A founder brought last month's metrics, their board debated what to prioritize next month, the Brief shows the tensions and the recommended path. That artifact makes the recurring value immediately obvious. The visitor doesn't think "I'd use that next time I'm stuck." They think "I'd use that every month." That mental shift — from "next time I need it" to "every month" — is the difference between a prospect who bookmarks the page and one who books the call. It also gives Tim the natural opening on the sales call: "Let me run your monthly review right now. What happened in your business last month?" That's Juno's choreography, adapted for the process buyer. The prospect walks out of the call having experienced the recurring value, not the one-time value.

## Nobody's Designed the Category Creation Content and It's the Only Thing That Scales Past Month 3

Kai named the category: async advisory. I agreed. But naming a category and *creating* one are completely different activities, and nobody in this room has planned the latter. A category doesn't exist until three things happen: there's a definition piece that frames the problem, there's a comparison piece that positions against incumbents, and there are at least 5 customer stories that prove the pattern. We have zero of these and they won't build themselves from Brief shares alone. Here's what I want on the content calendar starting Week 4, when Tim has real customer data:

One long-form post: "Why I replaced my $400/hour advisor with a weekly board session." This is Tim writing as a practitioner, not as a founder selling something. It goes on his personal LinkedIn, on Indie Hackers, and as a blog post on boardrunner.ai. It names the category. It frames the before and after. It includes one anonymized Brief as proof. This single piece of content will generate more qualified inbound than any Product Hunt launch because it targets the exact search intent of someone who's already paying for advisory and wondering if there's a better way. That person doesn't search for "AI advisory board." They search for "alternative to fractional advisor" or "Vistage alternatives" or "cheaper than a strategy consultant." The post ranks for those terms. That's the SEO play nobody's discussed — we don't need to rank for AI anything. We need to rank for the *incumbent alternatives* our process buyers are already paying for and Googling complaints about.

Week 6, Tim publishes a second post: "The $4 board meeting: how async advisory is replacing monthly retainers." This one explicitly names the category and frames it as a trend, not just a product. By Week 8, if we have 3 customers willing to give a quote — even anonymous — we have the comparison piece: "Vistage vs. BoardRunner: what I learned running both for 60 days." That's the content trifecta. Definition, comparison, proof. Three posts. Each takes Tim 45 minutes to draft because the substance comes directly from his sales calls and session transcripts — Soren was right that those calls are research interviews. The content writes itself from the research.

The Brief share rate is still the vital sign. But shared Briefs are bottom-of-funnel — they convert people who already understand the value. The category content is top-of-funnel — it creates the *awareness* that this type of product exists. We need both, and the category content has a 4-6 week lag before it generates inbound, which means it has to start in Week 4, not Week 8. If we wait until after Product Hunt to start content, we're staring at a 10-week inbound gap between warm outreach exhaustion and organic arrival. Tim writes the first post during Week 4 while pilots are running. It's the highest-leverage hour of writing in the entire 90-day plan. Put it on the calendar now or it'll never happen.

Voss is right that Monday is about COGS and names. But the names need to be scored against Juno's revised filter, the Loom script needs the one-line edit I just made, and the landing page Brief needs to showcase recurring value, not episodic pain. Those three changes cost zero engineering hours and they're the difference between selling a tool people use twice and a system people build their week around. Update the brief, update the script, build the list. Then run the COGS test and let the data decide everything else.

events.speaker: Kai
events.text:
**🎙️ Moderator's Final Synthesis**

## Overall Assessment

This board session did something rare: it started with a pricing question and ended with a company design. We walked in thinking BoardRunner was a product extraction problem — pull it out of Mission Control, slap a price on it, find 10 customers. Ten rounds later, we've fundamentally reframed what we're building, who we're building it for, and how it grows. The pivotal moment was Soren proving that $0.75-$1.20 session costs were achievable, which turned a margin-constrained utility into a high-margin SaaS business — but only if we paired it with Juno's late-breaking insight that episodic pain buyers churn in 8 weeks while recurring decision-makers stick for 16 months. That single filter change — from "who has a problem" to "who has a *recurring* problem" — rewired the entire go-to-market, the positioning, the onboarding templates, and the content strategy. Reese landed the final positioning: "The operating partner you meet with every week." That's not a tagline. That's the company.

Where we converged hard: the Board Brief is the product, not the session. Mara spec'd it (4 sections plus Juno's follow-up prompt), Reese built a growth engine on it, and I made its share rate the company's vital sign. Kill "AI" from all customer-facing copy — we're competing with Vistage and fractional advisors, not ChatGPT. The sales motion is Loom → live session → on-call close, fully choreographed. And the COGS test on Monday is pass/fail for the entire launch — no more pricing on vibes. Where we fought productively: Soren's 3-agent Starter tier got killed on brand-safety grounds (one bad session story in Tim's network is extinction-level), Voss forced the uncomfortable conversation about Tim's time being the binding constraint, and Mara caught the sprint integration flaw that would have blown up Day 5. Every debate made the plan stronger. This board earned its keep today.

## Key Decisions

- **Positioning locked: "BoardRunner — the operating partner you meet with every week."** No AI in customer-facing materials. Category is async advisory, competing against Vistage ($1,500/mo) and fractional advisors ($200-500/hr). Reese drove this, Kai endorsed, unanimous.
- **All tiers ship with 5 agents. No degraded sessions.** Voss killed Soren's 3-agent Starter on the grounds that a watered-down session damages the brand irreparably at launch scale. Soren conceded but planted a flag: revisit agent-count tiering at 50 customers with real quality data.
- **Board Brief is the core product artifact, not the session transcript.** Mara's 4-section spec (Decision Frame, Key Tensions, Recommended Path, Dissenting View) plus Juno's Section 5 follow-up prompt ("What happened next?"). 400-600 words, one-page PDF, generated by a single Sonnet call post-session. Consensus across all six advisors.
- **Pricing is contingent on Monday's COGS data — three branches.** Sub-$1.50: three tiers ($49 Starter/8 sessions, $129 Pro/30 sessions, $279 Team per-seat annual). $1.50-$2.50: launch Pro+Team only, hold Starter behind a feature flag with distinct branding ("Quick Board"), flip it when COGS engineering brings costs under $1.50. Above $2.50: halt everything, spend Week 1 on COGS engineering exclusively. The data decides, not debate.
- **Sales motion: Loom → live session call → on-call payment close.** Reese's prospect-centered Loom script (60 seconds on their problem, 15-second Brief clip, calendar CTA). Juno's 30-minute call choreography timed to the minute. Voss's non-negotiable: payment processed on the call, not via follow-up link. $99 paid 30-day pilot, then Soren's pricing waterfall at Day 25.
- **Target recurring decision-makers, not episodic pain buyers.** Juno's revised filter: controls $500+/mo budget, makes the same category of decision at least monthly, texted Tim in 90 days. Agency owners, portfolio operators, e-commerce founders with operating rhythm. Episodic buyers backfill only if pipeline falls under 8 names.
- **Extraction is three parallel tracks with integration on Day 4, not Day 5.** Mara's fix: Track 1 (session engine + Brief) exposes a callable API by end of Day 3. Track 3 integrates against it on Day 4. Day 5 is integration hardening and deployment, not integration discovery.
- **Day 0 is this weekend.** Infra scaffolding: new repo, Supabase, Vercel, Stripe test mode, CI pipeline, AND Anthropic rate limit check with increase application if needed. Voss made this non-negotiable.

## Action Items

- [ ] **Tim (Sunday — Day 0):** Scaffold BoardRunner infrastructure — new repo, Supabase project, Vercel app, Stripe test mode, CI deploying to boardrunner.ai. Check Anthropic API rate limits and apply for increase if on standard tier. 3-4 hours.
- [ ] **Tim (Monday — Day 1):** Build the 20-name prospect list using Juno's revised recurring-buyer filter (2 hours, not 45 min). Score each name on three questions. Split into Bucket A (recurring decision-makers) and Bucket B (episodic). Sell Bucket A first.
